title: MTA-STS policy discovery adapter: TXT lookup, HTTPS fetch, policy cache
description:
## What

pkix-mta-sts parses a policy and matches MX hosts. Discovery is not built: the `_mta-sts.<domain>` TXT lookup, the HTTPS GET of the policy, and the cache that makes MTA-STS protective at all.

Deferred from the core deliberately, not forgotten. It is a different kind of work -- a resolver, an HTTPS client, a cache with lifecycle rules -- and bundling it would have made one large change where two reviewable ones fit.

## Why the cache is the security mechanism, not an optimisation

Worth stating plainly because it inverts the usual reading. MTA-STS's TXT record is UNSIGNED and the policy is fetched over ordinary HTTPS, so first contact is trust-on-first-use and an attacker present at that moment wins. Everything MTA-STS protects comes from having cached a policy BEFORE the attacker arrives, for up to a year (§3.2 max_age).

So a half-built discovery layer that fetches correctly but caches sloppily provides approximately nothing while appearing to work. The cache is the feature.

## Pieces

TXT LOOKUP. `_mta-sts.<policy-domain>` TXT, parsed per §3.1: `v=STSv1; id=<policy-id>`. The id is an opaque change token -- when it differs from the cached one, refetch. No DNSSEC requirement, which is the whole trust-model difference from DANE. pkix-dane-resolver already has the resolver plumbing and the trust plumbing (RrsetTrust); reuse it rather than starting another, but note that MTA-STS does NOT need the DNSSEC validation DANE does, so requiring Secure here would refuse policies that are perfectly conforming.

HTTPS FETCH. `https://mta-sts.<policy-domain>/.well-known/mta-sts.txt`. §3.3 requirements that are easy to skip and matter:
  - The certificate MUST validate against the Web PKI for `mta-sts.<domain>`. A policy fetched over an unvalidated connection is worthless; this is the ONLY authentication the policy gets.
  - HTTP redirects MUST NOT be followed (§3.3). A followed redirect lets whoever controls the policy host move the fetch somewhere else.
  - Senders SHOULD validate the media type is text/plain (§3.2), "to guard against cases where web servers allow untrusted users to host non-text content at a user-defined path". The parser already rejects an HTML error page, and there is a test for that, but the media-type check is the intended first line.
  - SSRF: the hostname is derived from a caller-supplied domain. The fetch must not become a way to reach internal addresses.

CACHE. §5.1's control flow. Keyed by policy domain, holding the policy, its id, and the fetch time for `is_live_at`. Refetch when the TXT id changes or the policy expires. §5 also requires that an enforce-mode delivery failure "MUST NOT permanently fail to deliver messages before checking, via DNS, for the presence of an updated policy" -- so a bounce path has to consult DNS first, and the cache has to let it.

## Shape

Follow pkix-dane-resolver: a sans-IO core plus an async adapter, so the policy logic stays testable without a network. The pkix-revocation-http cache is the nearest precedent for a caller-supplied, now_unix-driven cache (it takes the instant rather than reading a clock, and there are tests asserting freshness is judged against the passed instant).

No filesystem and no OS dependency, per the workspace rule. The cache is caller-supplied storage, as pkix-revocation-http's is.

## Acceptance

[ ] `_mta-sts` TXT parsing per §3.1 including the policy id, with the id driving refetch
[ ] HTTPS fetch with Web PKI validation of `mta-sts.<domain>`, redirects refused, media type checked
[ ] A test that a redirect is NOT followed, and one that a non-text/plain body is refused
[ ] Cache keyed by policy domain with id-change and expiry invalidation, taking now_unix
[ ] A test that an enforce failure can consult DNS for an updated policy before bouncing (§5)
[ ] SSRF considerations documented, and the resolved address policy stated
[ ] Documented that DNSSEC is NOT required here, unlike DANE, and why requiring it would be wrong
close_reason:
DONE 2026-11-25. Two crates plus the cache rules in the no_std core. 85 tests across the three MTA-STS crates; 2163 workspace-wide, no failures.

## What shipped

pkix-mta-sts::discovery (no_std). §3.1 TXT record parsing and record selection, the CachedPolicy type, plan() for the §3.3/§5.1 control flow, policy_to_apply() for the post-fetch decision, and the name/URL construction.

pkix-mta-sts-http. PolicyFetcher (ureq) and AsyncPolicyFetcher (reqwest), every §3.3 requirement enforced, destination policy on by default.

pkix-net-guard. The destination policy, extracted from pkix-aia-http -- see below.

## The rules worth remembering

THE CACHE IS THE SECURITY MECHANISM. Stated in the filing and it held up. Two rules follow and both can be got backwards while the thing still appears to work:

  §3.1 -- an absent or unusable TXT record does NOT drop a cached policy
  §3.3 -- neither does a failed fetch, if the cached policy is still live

Either mistake lets an attacker strip up to a year of protection by suppressing one DNS answer or one HTTPS response. plan() returns UseCached, not NoPolicy, when the lookup failed and the cache is live, with a test per TXT failure mode.

LIVENESS AND REFRESH-DUE ARE DIFFERENT QUESTIONS. §3.3's proactive refresh is its own plan variant, not folded into expiry, because a policy can be both live and due. §10 is why it matters: an attacker who can block refresh indefinitely eventually outlasts any cached policy, so refreshing early shrinks the window they must control.

AMBIGUITY IS NOT RESOLVED BY PICKING ONE. Two MTA-STS TXT records means no policy, per §3.1. Which policy is current is exactly what the id exists to settle, so guessing defeats it. Non-MTA-STS records at the same name are discarded rather than fatal, so a domain publishing SPF at _mta-sts still works.

IDS COMPARE FOR EQUALITY ONLY. §3.1: "There is no implied ordering of id fields between revisions." A sender treating a lexically smaller id as older would be wrong on any domain using random ids. Documented on the accessor.

REDIRECTS ARE DISABLED, NOT CHECKED FOR. max_redirects(0) on the ureq agent and Policy::none() on the reqwest client. §3.3 says MUST NOT be followed, and the only way to be sure is to never allow one rather than to inspect the response afterwards.

## The extraction, and why it was not scope creep

pkix-aia-http already had this destination policy. Copying it would have duplicated the subtle part: IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible and NAT64 well-known-prefix addresses judged by their embedded IPv4 address, because ::ffff:127.0.0.1 is loopback to the kernel but is not an Ipv4Addr, and missing that is the standard filter bypass. Plus RFC 6598, 0.0.0.0/8, 240.0.0.0/4, deprecated IPv6 site-local.

Depending on pkix-aia-http instead would have dragged all of certificate parsing in for an address filter, and left a dependency edge from MTA-STS to AIA that no reader could explain.

A second concrete consumer is when extraction stops being speculative, so it was the right moment. pkix-aia-http's public API is unchanged (both resolvers re-exported) and its 40 tests pass untouched.

It also found a duplication that was already there: pkix-aia-http defined the reqwest resolver in async_fetcher.rs separately from the ureq one in lib.rs, two copies of the same decision differing in error construction. They now share refusal_message, so an operator reading a log cannot tell which backend refused.

## Testing the untestable part

A policy fetch is HTTPS-only, so the usual local-HTTP-server integration test does not apply without a TLS server and a trusted cert. Two things made it testable anyway:

  - check_status and check_media_type are pure, shared by both backends, and now public, so the §3.3 and §3.2 rules are asserted directly rather than through a transport.
  - mta-sts.localhost resolves to loopback on a normal system -- exactly where an attacker would steer a sender -- and the guard refuses inside the resolver, before any connection. So the destination policy IS testable end to end with no server at all.

The complement matters as much as the test: with the guard off the same fetch fails as transport instead, which proves the refusal came from the guard rather than from nothing listening. Both backends, because they use different resolver traits and a guard applied to one would leave the other open while looking covered.

## Acceptance

[x] _mta-sts TXT parsing per §3.1 including the policy id, with the id driving refetch
[x] HTTPS fetch with Web PKI validation of mta-sts.<domain>, redirects refused, media type checked
[x] A test that a redirect is NOT followed -- via check_status over every 3xx, plus redirects disabled on the client
[x] A test that a non-text/plain body is refused
[x] Cache keyed by policy domain with id-change and expiry invalidation, taking now_unix
[x] SSRF considerations documented, and the resolved address policy stated
[x] Documented that DNSSEC is NOT required here, unlike DANE
[~] The §5 "consult DNS before permanently failing" path: plan() supports it (a caller re-runs it and gets Fetch on an id change) but there is no dedicated bounce-path helper, because bouncing is the MTA's decision and this layer does not own it. Noted rather than claimed.

## Not done

The policy cache STORAGE. plan() and policy_to_apply() are the rules; where a policy is kept is the caller's, because the workspace does not depend on a filesystem or an OS. A caller enables the serde feature and persists CachedPolicy.

§3.3's five-minute per-version-ID failure backoff. The constant is exported (SUGGESTED_FETCH_BACKOFF_SECS) and documented, but rate-limiting belongs with the cache storage, so it goes wherever that does.
